analysis.one_liner: Restricts payday-style online lenders from draining bank accounts, evading state rate caps, and selling borrowers' financial data.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote in the Senate Banking Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted the online small-dollar lending industry. It would let borrowers revoke any lender's permission to pull payments from their bank account, ban remotely created checks a borrower never authorized, ban overdraft fees on prepaid cards, make online lenders obey the interest rate caps of the state where the borrower lives (closing the loophole where lenders partner with a bank in a different state to charge more), require lenders to register with the consumer bureau, and stop companies from selling borrowers' bank account and Social Security numbers through lead generators. It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee and never went anywhere.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income borrowers who use payday, installment, or prepaid products. The people most likely to take out a $500 online loan at triple-digit rates, or to get hit with an overdraft fee on a prepaid card, are working people living paycheck to paycheck. Under the bill, their state's rate caps would apply to online loans, unauthorized withdrawals from their accounts would be blocked, and their bank details could not be sold to anonymous lead-generation middlemen.

how_it_helps.text: Bans overdraft fees on prepaid accounts — a fee a person gets charged for spending money they didn't have in an account that isn't even a bank account.

Bars lenders from debiting a borrower's bank account using remotely created checks unless the borrower specifically authorized that lender in writing, and lets the borrower revoke that permission at any time — a direct answer to the unlicensed debits common in online payday lending.

Extends the same legal protections to any one-time electronic debit that currently apply only to recurring preauthorized transfers, closing a gap lenders used to withdraw payments in ways borrowers couldn't stop.

Requires online small-dollar lenders to follow the interest rate and fee laws of the state where the borrower lives, shutting off the channel they have used to evade state rate caps by operating through a bank in another state.

Requires small-dollar lenders to register with the consumer bureau before making loans, and stops companies from selling borrowers' sensitive financial information (bank account and routing numbers, Social Security numbers) to lead generators they can't be identified and sued.

analysis.who_pays: Payday and online small-dollar lenders, lead generators, and prepaid card providers would lose revenue: no overdraft fees on prepaid accounts, no debit-based collections without explicit consumer authorization, no evasion of state rate caps through national bank partnerships, and no selling of borrowers' sensitive financial data unless they are the actual lender.
analysis.who_pays_short: Payday lenders, lead generators, prepaid card issuers

drawbacks.text: Requiring small-dollar loans made online to follow the consumer's home state rate rules could push some lenders to stop offering credit in states with tight rate caps, reducing access to short-term credit for borrowers there who feel they need it.
The registration and reporting requirements add compliance costs for small lenders, which could shrink the number of legitimate providers and concentrate the market among larger companies.
The bill relies on the consumer bureau to write the detailed rules within a year, so the real-world strength of the protections would depend on how those rules are written and enforced.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits for low-income borrowers — fewer surprise fees, no unlicensed debits, loans subject to their state's rate caps — outweigh the costs, which fall on a small-dollar lending industry that profits from exactly the practices the bill targets. Legitimate lenders would face registration and state-law compliance, some of which could reduce the supply of small-dollar credit in high-cost states; that is the strongest good-faith objection, though the bill's GAO study of lending on tribal lands acknowledges the need to preserve access to credit, not just restrict it. The bill died before any of this was debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced and never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill's entire action history is two lines: introduced in the Senate on September 19, 2024, and read twice and referred to the Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee the same day.
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred; the Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill died there.
It had 10 cosponsors, all Democrats or allied independents, so it would have faced an uphill path in the Senate even if the committee had acted.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Online small-dollar lenders, lead generators, and prepaid card issuers keep charging the fees and making the withdrawals the bill would have restricted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Online payday lenders and lead generators

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led its promotion.

for.name: Sens. Baldwin, Blumenthal, Wyden, Van Hollen, Sanders, Durbin, Markey, Heinrich, and Smith
for.role: Cosponsors (9 Democrats plus Sen. King, I)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it a full Democratic slate but no Republican support.

against.name: Small-dollar lending industry
against.what_they_did: The bill's provisions directly target this industry's core practices; it faced industry opposition as a category, though no group's action is recorded in the provided sources.

against.name: Senate Banking Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, markup, or vote — which by itself prevented the bill from advancing.

sides.party_line_note: All 10 cosponsors were Democrats or an allied independent; no Republican signed on, and with the bill referred only to committee it never had to survive a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill's core targets are this industry's practices: unlicensed account debits, evasion of state rate caps through bank partnerships, and anonymous lead generation. A registration requirement would bring the whole sector under direct federal oversight.

The bill bans selling consumers' bank account and Social Security numbers in connection with small-dollar loans unless the company is itself the lender, ending a lucrative side business built on sensitive data.
Prepaid overdraft fees would be banned, cutting a revenue stream some programs rely on, though the underlying product remains legal.

industries.industry: Banks originating loans for online lenders
industries.note: The provision applying the borrower's home state rate rules to loans made by national banks threatens the 'rent-a-bank' arrangement some banks use to originate high-rate loans for online lenders.
